name: Ghost River State Natural Area
company: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
unique: A 2,306 acre stretch of the Wolf River where the channel splits into braided sloughs and tupelo and cypress swamp, held as a Class I scenic-recreational natural area so the bottomland forest within half an hour of Memphis stays flooded, tangled and mostly empty.
buzz: People who paddle it talk about the cypress knees and the silence rather than any facility. Bring a map, because the braids all look alike and the current does the steering.

name: Wolf River Bottomland Paddle
dates: Spring through fall, water level dependent
company: Free / self-guided, rentals from Memphis outfitters
unique: A slow current through drowned forest where the only signs of people are the white blazes on trees, with sandbars for stopping and enough dead water that a beginner can handle it.
buzz: Outfitters run shuttles from the Memphis side. Paddlers warn about strainers after storms and say the fall color on the tupelo is the best in west Tennessee.

name: Somerville Court Square
unique: A National Register courthouse square in the middle of horse country, with the 1870s courthouse on the lawn, a gazebo, and a ring of shops that serve a county of soybean fields and training barns.
buzz: The square is small and intact, and the cafes around it are where the horse farms eat. People come for the Christmas lights and stay for the pie.

name: Fayette County Cotton Festival
unique: A one day courthouse square festival that keeps the county's cotton economy in the name, with a tractor display, vendor booths, live music and a barbecue that runs out before the afternoon.
buzz: Regulars describe it as the county's homecoming, where the vendors are neighbors and the square is packed from ten in the morning. The food lines are the long ones.

name: Wolf River Cafe
dates: Breakfast and lunch daily, dinner some evenings
unique: A country cafe in a two stoplight town that still cooks catfish, turnip greens and biscuits the way the surrounding farms eat, with a plate lunch that changes daily and a table of regulars who arrive at six.
buzz: Reviews keep coming back to the catfish plate, the tomato relish and the feeling of eating in somebody's grandmother's dining room. Portions are large and the prices are not city prices.

name: Herb Parsons Lake
customer: Anglers, paddlers, families with small children
unique: A 177 acre TWRA lake named for Herb Parsons, the Winchester exhibition shooter from Memphis who could break six targets with a rifle in under a second, with a fishing pier, a boat ramp and bank access in the woods north of Collierville.
buzz: Anglers fish it for bass, crappie and catfish and call it the closest quiet water to the eastern suburbs. The name gets a story out of anybody who shoots.

name: Tipton County Museum, Veterans Memorial and Nature Center
unique: One building with three jobs: county history and a period room, a veterans memorial wall with names from every war, and a nature center with live snakes and turtles backed by a twenty acre hardwood sanctuary and a half mile trail.
buzz: Locals bring grandchildren for the animals and end up reading the veterans wall. It is free, air conditioned and the trail behind it is the surprise.

name: World's Oldest BBQ Contest
cost: Free entry, food priced per item
unique: A competition that has run since 1973 and claims the oldest continuous barbecue contest in the country, held at Cobb-Parr Park with a rodeo, a truck and tractor pull, and teams cooking shoulder and ribs for judges and for anybody standing in line.
buzz: The claim is on the banner and the locals defend it. Reviews call it a small town fair with serious barbecue, and the teams come back every year.

name: Randolph
customer: History buffs, back road drivers, photographers
unique: A river landing where a town that outshipped Memphis in cotton until the 1840s is now a church, a cemetery, a marker and a bluff over the Mississippi, with the levee and the sandbars doing the talking.
buzz: People come for the ghost town story and stay for the river view. The bluff is high enough that the river looks like a lake, and there is nobody there.

name: Ruffin Theater
unique: A 1930s movie house on Covington's square with a 640 seat auditorium and a neon marquee, kept alive as a live venue and community stage rather than a cinema.
buzz: The room is the draw. People who grew up seeing movies there now bring their own children to shows, and the marquee is the photo on the way into town.

name: Atoka Railroad Adventure
unique: A railroad themed family park built around a miniature train ride, with go karts, miniature golf and an indoor arcade, close enough to Memphis that it works as a half day out rather than a trip.
buzz: Parents describe it as small, cheap and easy with young children, and note that the train is the thing the kids ask about again.

name: Covington Court Square
unique: A courthouse square with a 1930s movie marquee and a ring of storefronts that still includes a working hardware store, in the seat of a county that grows cotton, corn and soybeans on the loess bluffs above the Mississippi.
buzz: Covington's square is where the county gathers. The barbecue festival fills it and the rest of the year it is a good place to park and walk two blocks.

name: West Tennessee Delta Heritage Center
customer: Music fans, families, road trippers on Interstate 40
unique: A free welcome center and museum off the interstate that treats west Tennessee's music and cotton culture as one story, with the Tina Turner Museum in a restored one room schoolhouse, the last home of Sleepy John Estes, and exhibits on the Delta that do not soften the labor history.
buzz: People stop for a bathroom break and leave an hour later. The schoolhouse and the blues house are the two things everybody photographs, and the staff know which local musician is playing where.

name: Tina Turner Museum at Flagg Grove School
customer: Music fans, Tina Turner pilgrims, school groups
unique: The only Tina Turner museum anywhere, inside the one room schoolhouse Anna Mae Bullock attended as a girl in Nutbush, with costumes, gold records, stage clothes and the story of leaving a cotton town for Ike, then for everything else.
buzz: Fans drive from Memphis and from Europe, and the volunteers say the guest book fills with names from a dozen countries. The schoolhouse desks are the part people did not expect.

name: Sleepy John Estes Home
unique: The last house of the country blues singer who named Brownsville in his songs, moved to the heritage center grounds and kept as a plain one story frame house rather than a shrine.
buzz: Blues travellers treat it as a stop on the same road as the Mississippi graves and juke joints. The plainness is what they comment on, a sharecropper's house next to an interstate exit.

name: Hatchie National Wildlife Refuge
dates: Year round, daylight; some roads flood in winter
unique: Eleven thousand acres of Hatchie River bottomland, the last free flowing river of its kind in the region, managed for wintering waterfowl with moist soil units, blinds and a launch where the cypress and buttonbush close in.
buzz: Birders come for the winter duck concentration and the spring migrants. Locals warn that the lower roads go under after heavy rain, which is also why the place is as quiet as it is.

name: Brownsville Court Square
unique: A wide square with a 1930s courthouse and a bandstand, in a town that was a cotton market and still holds a summer concert series on the lawn.
buzz: The square is five minutes from the interstate and almost nobody from out of town stops. Those who do find a diner, a law office row and a good place to eat lunch.

name: Fort Pillow State Historic Park
unique: A 1,642 acre park on the Chickasaw Bluffs where the earthworks of a Confederate fort still stand above the Mississippi, and where the April 1864 battle ended in the massacre of Black Union soldiers after they surrendered, a story the museum tells plainly with artifacts and a film.
buzz: Visitors say the bluff view and the preserved breastworks are the best Civil War earthworks in the state, and that the museum does not soften what happened there. Reenactments draw crowds in spring and fall.

name: Alex Haley House Museum and Interpretive Center
unique: The ten room bungalow where Alex Haley spent his boyhood hearing the family stories that became Roots, with original Haley furniture and, behind it, an interpretive center with a walk through exhibit on the slave trade, the Middle Passage and the search that led him to the Gambia.
buzz: The house is the emotional part and the center is the research part. Visitors mention the grapevine story and the grave on the grounds, and genealogists come to use the room set aside for tracing families.

name: Lauderdale County Museum
dates: Weekdays and some Saturdays, call ahead
unique: A county collection inside Sugar Hill, an 1842 mansion with a two story portico, holding the ordinary things that explain a river county: cotton ledgers, uniforms, quilts, photographs and the records of the towns that washed away.
buzz: Small and volunteer run, and the volunteers are the ones who know which family owned which house. Visitors who call ahead get a tour that lasts twice as long as they planned.

name: Lauderdale County Courthouse
unique: A 1936 Public Works Administration courthouse of buff glazed brick on a cruciform plan with an inlaid terrazzo map of the county in the rotunda, one of the more unusual of Tennessee's Depression era courthouses.
buzz: Courthouse chasers put it on the short list for the terrazzo map alone. Everyone else is in Ripley for the museum and walks in not knowing what is under their feet.

name: Lauderdale County Tomato Festival
unique: A two day July festival built around the tomato growers of the Mississippi bottomland, with a tomato contest and tasting, a five kilometer run, a carnival and the naming of the Tomato Farmer of the Year at the opening ceremony.
buzz: It is the county's biggest weekend and the tasting table is the reason people come early. The royalty contest and the carnival rides are the parts the children remember.

name: Veterans' Museum at Dyersburg Army Air Base
dates: Weekdays and weekend afternoons, call ahead
company: Dyersburg Army Air Base Memorial Association
unique: A museum on the concrete of a World War Two B-17 combat crew training base, where thousands of airmen learned to fly before shipping out, with a restored hangar building, engine parts, uniforms and the names of the crews who did not come home.
buzz: Aviation people come for the base history and find the personal collections more affecting. Volunteers are often veterans themselves and will talk for as long as you let them.

name: Lauderdale County Fair
customer: Families, farm families, demolition derby crowds
unique: A small county fair that still runs livestock shows, a barbecue cook off, ATV and mini tractor pulls, wrestling, a car show and Choctaw social dancing, all in one weekend at the end of August.
buzz: The pulls and the derby are what fill the grandstand. People describe it as a fair that has not been smoothed out for outsiders, which is the appeal.

name: National Bird Dog Museum
dates: Tue-Fri and weekend afternoons, closed Monday
customer: Field trial people, dog owners, curious road trippers
unique: A museum to pointing dogs and retrievers with oil paintings of champions, field trial trophies, mounted birds and the records of a century of competitive hunting, in a town of a few hundred people that happens to be the capital of the sport.
buzz: People arrive expecting a joke and leave impressed by the paintings and the seriousness of the field trial world. The hall of fame plaques and the dog art are the two things mentioned most.

name: National Championship Field Trial
company: National Field Trial Champion Association at Ames Plantation
customer: Field trial followers, dog people, the merely curious
unique: The National Championship has been decided on the same Ames Plantation grounds since 1915, with horseback handlers, judges following on horseback, and pointers and setters run in braces across thousands of acres of west Tennessee cover.
buzz: Spectators follow in a gallery on horseback or in wagons and the whole thing is free. First timers are surprised by how formal and quiet it is, and by how far the dogs range.

name: Little Courthouse Museum
unique: A two story log courthouse built in 1824 with a courtroom below and a jail room above, later hauled down the street and turned into a house, now holding Hardeman County relics including a chair said to have belonged to Jefferson Davis.
buzz: The building is the exhibit. Volunteers have been working to reopen it on regular hours, so call first, and the people who get inside talk about the log walls and the stairs.

name: Country Cabin Music Museum
unique: A private museum of country and gospel music run by a couple in a small town, with instruments, stage clothes, records and photographs accumulated over decades of shows, and a stage where visiting pickers still play.
buzz: Visitors describe being walked through the collection personally by the owners. It is the kind of place that exists because two people never threw anything away.

name: Bolivar Court Square and Historic District
unique: A courthouse square with an 1870s courthouse on a hill above the shops, in a town that was a staging point for both armies and later a furniture and cotton center, with a historic district of brick storefronts around it.
buzz: Quiet and intact. The square is where you eat before the Little Courthouse, and the houses uphill are worth the loop.

name: Davis Bridge Battlefield
unique: The Hatchie River crossing where on October 5, 1862, Union troops caught the retreating Confederate army after Corinth and fought for the bridge, with earthworks, a marker and a wide bend of river that still looks like the reason the fight happened.
buzz: Barely developed and rarely crowded, which is exactly what battlefield walkers like about it. The ground is the point, so bring the map and read before you go.
